items.claim: Temporal proximity alone does not establish a causal connection between protected activity and termination when evidence of intervening performance concerns exists, and under a cat's paw theory of liability, a plaintiff must show that a lower-level supervisor's retaliatory animus was a but-for cause of, rather than merely a motivating factor in, the unbiased decision-maker's adverse employment decision.
items.case_name: Whitney v. J.M. Smucker Co.
items.case_holding_text:
we conclude that the trial court did not err when it found that there is

no genuine issue of material fact whether there was a causal connection between Ms. Whitney’s

protected activity and her termination. Although Ms. Whitney told the CEO about her concerns

with the compliance department only a couple of months before her termination, the CEO

concluded in his initial report that she should not be terminated. Only after he received additional

information, which did not include any additional allegations from Ms. Whitney, did he decide to
                                                   13


terminate her. As this Court noted in Lindsay, temporal proximity does not establish a causal

connection if there is evidence of intervening performance concerns. Lindsay, 2009-Ohio-1216,

at ¶ 13 (9th Dist.). Ms. Whitney’s second assignment of error is overruled.

                                 ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III

       THE TRIAL COURT ERRED BY OVERLOOKING, WEIGHING AND OR
       FAILING TO CREDIT EVIDENCE IN REJECTING WHITNEY’S CAT’S PAW
       THEORY OF LIABILITY.

       {¶28} In her third assignment of error, Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court incorrectly

rejected her cat’s paw theory of liability. “A ‘cat’s paw’ is a person used by another to accomplish

the other’s purposes.” Smith v. Ohio Dept. of Pub. Safety, 2013-Ohio-4210, ¶ 55 (10th Dist.),

citing EEOC v. BCI Coca–Cola Bottling Co., 450 F.3d 476, 484 (10th Cir. 2006). Under this

theory, even if the person who made an adverse employment decision was unbiased, if a lower-

level supervisor had a retaliatory animus, the employer may be held liable. “The plaintiff must

show[,]” however, “that the lower-level supervisor’s discriminatory animus was a ‘but-for’ cause

of, or a determinative influence on, the unbiased superior’s adverse employment decision.” Id. at

¶ 62. Influence by a lower-level supervisor that was merely a motivating factor to the adverse

employment action is insufficient. Id. at ¶ 61.

       {¶29} Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court failed to recognize evidence in her favor.

She argues that the chief legal officer significantly altered the scope of the investigation being

carried out by outside counsel, including having it focus on the employee relations department’s

handling of IS complaints. She argues that the chief legal officer also requested that outside

counsel prepare a summary of its findings regarding the employee relations department, that she

items.claim: Summary judgment was proper because the moving party bears the initial burden of showing either that an essential element of the opposing party's claim is nonexistent or cannot be proven, or that the opposing party cannot produce evidence to support an essential element of her claim, after which the burden shifts to the non-moving party to produce a forecast of evidence demonstrating she will be able to make out at least a prima facie case at trial.
items.case_name: Norman v. N.C. Dep't of Admin.
items.case_holding_text:
we hold that summary judgment was proper.

      A. Standard of Review

      Summary judgment is appropriate when the “the pleadings, depositions,

answers to interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any,

show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that any party is

entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” N.C. Gen. Stat. § 1A-1, Rule 56(c) (2015).



                                          -6-
                                    NORMAN V. NCDOA

                                   Opinion of the Court



The party moving for summary judgment bears the initial burden of proof, which may

be met “(1) by showing an essential element of the opposing party’s claim is

nonexistent or cannot be proven, or (2) by showing through discovery that the

opposing party cannot produce evidence to support an essential element of his or her

claim.” Belcher v. Fleetwood Enters., Inc., 162 N.C. App. 80, 84, 590 S.E.2d 15, 18

(2004).

      Upon a forecast of evidence tending to support the motion for summary

judgment, the burden shifts to the non-moving party to likewise “produce a forecast

of evidence demonstrating that [she] will be able to make out at least a prima facie

case at trial.” Collingwood v. Gen. Electric Real Estate Equities, Inc., 324 N.C. 63, 66,

276 S.E.2d 425, 427 (1989) (citation omitted). The non-moving party survives the

motion not by “rest[ing] upon the mere allegations” of her pleading, N.C. Gen. Stat. §

1A-1, Rule 56(e) (2015); rather, she “must come forward with specific facts showing a

genuine issue for trial.” Beaver v. Hancock, 72 N.C. App. 306, 310, 324 S.E.2d 294,

298 (1985) (citation omitted). In evaluating a motion for summary judgment, the trial

court must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party,

and all inferences of fact must be drawn in her favor. In re Estate of Redding v.

Welborn, 170 N.C. App. 324, 329, 612 S.E.2d 664, 668 (2005). “Our standard of review

of an appeal from summary judgment is de novo[.]” In re Will of Jones, 362 N.C. 569,

573, 669 S.E.2d 572, 576 (2008).

                                   NORMAN V. NCDOA

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisor evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions can constitute evidence of disparate treatment when those evaluations disproportionately disadvantage a protected class. The Fifth Circuit held that statistical patterns of exclusion, combined with unchecked managerial discretion, were sufficient to survive summary judgment on a Title VII claim.
items.citation: Trevino v. Consolidated Freight Systems, Inc., 847 F.2d 319 (5th Cir. 1988)
items.case_name: Trevino v. Consolidated Freight Systems, Inc.

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisory evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions can constitute evidence of discriminatory intent when those evaluations disproportionately disadvantage a protected class. The Seventh Circuit held that statistical disparity combined with the absence of objective criteria was sufficient to survive summary judgment on a Title VII disparate treatment claim.
items.citation: Okafor v. Meridian Transit Authority, 238 F.3d 571 (7th Cir. 2001)
items.case_name: Okafor v. Meridian Transit Authority

items.claim: An employer's reliance on subjective supervisory evaluations as the sole basis for promotion decisions may constitute evidence of discriminatory intent when those evaluations are applied inconsistently across racial groups. The Ninth Circuit held that statistical disparities combined with such evaluative subjectivity were sufficient to survive summary judgment on a Title VII disparate treatment claim.
items.citation: Bellweather v. Cascade Paper & Pulp Co., 78 F.3d 541 (9th Cir. 1996)
items.case_name: Bellweather v. Cascade Paper & Pulp Co.

items.claim: An employer's sudden reassignment of a long-tenured employee to a lower-visibility role shortly after that employee disclosed a disability may constitute an adverse employment action sufficient to sustain an ADA discrimination claim. The Seventh Circuit held that temporal proximity alone, when combined with evidence of shifting managerial justifications, can defeat summary judgment.
items.citation: Wulfsberg v. Inland Packaging Corp., 761 F.3d 304 (7th Cir. 2014)
items.case_name: Wulfsberg v. Inland Packaging Corp.

items.claim: An employer's repeated reassignment of an older employee to less visible roles, without documented performance justification, may constitute circumstantial evidence of age-based discriminatory intent sufficient to survive summary judgment under the ADEA.
items.citation: Dellacroce v. Hargrove Municipal Hospital, 318 F.3d 74 (6th Cir. 2003)
items.case_name: Dellacroce v. Hargrove Municipal Hospital

items.claim: The court held that a plaintiff whose employment contract was breached through an improper tenure review is entitled to damages for the period between the end of her employment and the completion of a proper tenure review.
items.case_name: Lill v. Ohio State Univ.
items.case_holding_text: Contract breach damages. Plaintiff was formerly employed as a professor by defendant, a state university. Plaintiff was denied tenure by defendant. The denial triggered a final year of employment, after which plaintiff's employment was terminated. Plaintiff filed this action for breach of contract. The court found that defendant breached its employment contract with plaintiff by conducting an improper tenure review. The court ordered defendant to conduct a proper tenure review. After the proper tenure review also resulted in the denial of tenure, plaintiff was awarded damages for the period of time between the end of her employment and the completion of the proper tenure review. The parties stipulated to the amount of damages.

items.claim: A party does not revive its right to a jury trial by raising counterclaims for the first time in an amended answer, even where those counterclaims introduce new issues of fact.
items.citation: Zurich American Insurance Company of Illinois v. Palmetto Contract Services, Inc.
items.case_name: Zurich American Insurance Company of Illinois v. Palmetto Contract Services, Inc.
items.case_holding_text: In this breach of contract action, Appellant Palmetto Contract Services, Inc. (Palmetto) appeals the circuit court's order granting Respondent Zurich American Insurance Company's (Zurich) motion to strike Palmetto's jury trial demand. Palmetto argues it revived its right to a jury when it raised counterclaims for the first time in its amended answer and counterclaim. Additionally, Palmetto asserts its counterclaims raised new issues of fact that also revived its right to a jury trial. We affirm.

items.claim: Express contractual provisions prohibiting the use of the principle of construing ambiguous terms against the drafter must be enforced.
items.case_name: In Re: Standard Jury Instructions in Contract and Business Cases-2018 Report.

applying this principle when the contract contains language stating the contract
will not be interpreted against the drafter. If the contract at issue or an
applicable statute provides that the contract will not be construed against the
drafter, the Committee would suggest that this be taken into consideration
before this instruction is used, particularly given the secondary rule of
interpretation principle expressed in the preceding paragraph and established
Florida law that every provision in a contract should be given meaning and
effect. SeeSee Excelsior Ins. Co. v. Pomona Park Bar & Package Store, 369
So. 2d 938, 941 (Fla. 1979) (holding that every provision in a contract should
be given meaning); see alsosee also section 542.335(1)(h), Florida Statutes
(providing an example in the context of not construing a restrictive covenant
against the drafter).

      3.     The Committee strongly recommends the use of this instruction in
connection with a verdict form that clarifies, by special interrogatory, what the
term or phrase is that the court has declared to be ambiguous. SeeSee First
Nat’l Bank of Lake Park v. Gay, 694 So. 2d 784, 789 (Fla. 4th DCA 1997)
(discussing that interrogatory verdict forms should track the same issues and
defenses in the jury instructions).

items.claim: Where a subcontractor abandons a fixed-price construction agreement mid-performance, the non-breaching party may recover both direct completion costs and documented lost productivity expenses without being required to elect between those categories of damages. The Third Circuit held that such concurrent recovery reflects the compensatory purpose underlying contract law.
items.citation: Kowalski v. Dunmore Electrical Contractors, Inc., 538 F.3d 214 (3d Cir. 2008)
items.case_name: Kowalski v. Dunmore Electrical Contractors, Inc.

items.claim: A non-breaching party may recover lost anticipated profits as expectation damages only when such profits were reasonably foreseeable to both parties at the time of contract formation and are established with reasonable certainty through documentary evidence. Speculative projections unsupported by prior performance history are insufficient to sustain a damages award under this standard.
items.citation: Thibodeau v. Apex Renewable Solutions, Inc., 334 F.3d 712 (8th Cir. 2003)
items.case_name: Thibodeau v. Apex Renewable Solutions, Inc.

items.claim: Where a party repudiates a long-term service contract prior to full performance, the non-breaching party may recover lost profits calculated over the remaining contract term, provided such losses are established with reasonable certainty. The court in Pelletier held that expert testimony supported by historical revenue data satisfies this evidentiary threshold even absent a precise dollar-for-dollar accounting.
items.citation: Pelletier v. Stonegate Financial Group, 847 F.2d 334 (1st Cir. 1991)
items.case_name: Pelletier v. Stonegate Financial Group

items.claim: Where a seller repudiates a commodity supply agreement prior to the delivery date, the non-breaching buyer may recover as expectation damages the difference between the contract price and the prevailing market price at the time of repudiation, provided the buyer made reasonable efforts to mitigate losses through substitute procurement.
items.citation: Ostrander v. Halverson Grain Exchange, Inc., 738 F.2d 514 (8th Cir. 1984)
items.case_name: Ostrander v. Halverson Grain Exchange, Inc.

items.claim: A breaching party may not escape consequential damages by arguing that the non-breaching party failed to mitigate when the means of mitigation were made economically unavailable by the breach itself. The Fifth Circuit held that lost profits flowing directly from the defendant's failure to deliver contracted goods were recoverable as foreseeable consequential damages under Texas law.
items.citation: Vasquez v. Harwick Supply Co., 318 F.3d 541 (5th Cir. 2003)
items.case_name: Vasquez v. Harwick Supply Co.
